wstep: This card describes how to dry chanterelles reliably identified as edible in a dehydrator or oven at 140 °F (60 °C), without blanching.

ostrzezenia.tekst: Drying and cooking do not destroy the toxins of poisonous mushrooms, and only an expert can tell edible species from poisonous ones.
Dry only cultivated or wild mushrooms that are safe to eat; unless you are an expert in mushroom identification, preserve only commercially sold mushrooms.

In Poland: if in doubt whether mushrooms are edible, take them fresh, before drying, to a sanitary-epidemiological station (sanepid); mushroom experts or classifiers there assess free of charge whether they are edible, inedible or poisonous.

akapity: Outside Poland this card does not name an institution that assesses mushrooms: if you are not sure a mushroom is edible, do not dry or eat it.
Take whole fruiting bodies, with cap and stem, for assessment, because important identifying features are also on the stem; so have the mushrooms assessed before slicing and drying.
In Poland, a mushroom expert (grzyboznawca) is authorised to assess whether fresh and dried mushrooms are fit to eat.
According to OSU, most mushrooms dry well, including chanterelles.
Scrub the mushrooms.
Discard tough, woody stalks and slice tender stalks 1/4 inch thick.
Peel large mushrooms and slice them; leave small mushrooms whole.
Dip the mushrooms for 10 minutes in a solution of 1 teaspoon citric acid per 1 quart of water, then drain.
Do not blanch the mushrooms.
Arrange the prepared mushrooms on trays in a single or thin layer, no more than 1/2 inch (about 13 mm) deep.
Dry the mushrooms at 140 °F (60 °C) in a dehydrator or oven.
Do not dry mushrooms outdoors: dry them under the controlled conditions of an oven or dehydrator.
Do not use trays or screens made of galvanized mesh; also avoid copper and aluminium mesh.
Only use an oven if it can be set as low as 140 °F (60 °C); if it cannot go that low, the mushrooms cook instead of drying.
In an oven, keep 140–150 °F (about 60–66 °C): place a calibrated oven thermometer on the rack or tray and check it every 2 hours throughout drying.
Leave the oven door open 2–3 inches (about 5–7.5 cm) so moisture can escape.
In a conventional oven, drying can take up to twice as long as in a dehydrator, depending on air circulation.
Dry the mushrooms for 8–12 hours, until dry and leathery.
The Polish Minister of Health reminds people to eat only edible mushrooms that have been heat-treated, such as fried or cooked.
Pack only completely cooled mushrooms: warm dried food sweats, and that moisture can be enough for mould to grow.
Store the dried mushrooms in clean, dry canning jars, plastic freezer containers with tight-fitting lids or plastic freezer bags.
Keep the dried food in airtight containers so it does not absorb moisture from the air: dry foods kept out of airtight containers may absorb moisture.
Packaging must be food grade: do not use trash bags or plastic or fibreboard containers that previously held non-food items.
Pack amounts that can be used at one time: each opening exposes the dried food to air and moisture, which lowers quality and can lead to spoilage.
Vacuum packaging is not a preservation method by itself: removing oxygen increases the risk of botulism, and a product that needs refrigeration still needs it.
Store the dried mushrooms in a cool, dry, dark place.
Check the dried vegetables often (glass shows condensation); if they have taken up moisture but are not spoiled, use them at once or dry them again and repack them.
Throw away mouldy dried vegetables; also throw away any that smell off.

With the most dangerous mushrooms, such as the death cap, the first symptoms often appear long after eating, sometimes only after several days, and after a temporary improvement the condition can worsen rapidly; with symptoms of poisoning, call a doctor at once or go to hospital, and seek help also for people who ate the same dish even if they have no symptoms yet.
